title: VIPR RNA-guided DNA recognition by noncontiguous geometric triplex formation.
data_url: https://www.rcsb.org/search?request=%7B%22citation_doi%22%3A%2210.1126/science.aei3472%22%7D (18 PDB entries: 35SE, 35SF, 35SG, 35SY, 35TR, 35TW, 35TX, 36PB, 36PC, 36PD, 36PE, 36PF, 36PG, 36PJ, 36PK, 36PM, 36PO, 36PR; maps EMD-77155 to EMD-77745)

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Queried the RCSB (Protein Data Bank) search API by this paper's DOI: exactly 18 deposited atomic models, all cryo-electron microscopy, 2.5-3.5 Angstrom, 282,173 atoms in total, each linked to one EMDB (Electron Microscopy Data Bank) map. Downloaded and parsed two of them: 35SE.cif (959,256 bytes; Vipr protein 202 amino acids plus a 29-nucleotide guide RNA) and 36PG.cif (2,084,876 bytes; 94-nucleotide guide RNA, two 63-nucleotide DNA strands, 11 protein copies). Also checked Zenodo: the only related deposit is Doudna-Lab/VIPR_analysis_scripts (139,288-byte zip, software only, tagged ChIP-seq and Evo2), which belongs to the companion discovery paper, not this one.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The abstract's claim of 21 cryo-EM structures (I verified 18 with atomic models). The Science full text, methods and supplementary materials are paywalled: Europe PMC marks the paper closed-access with no PMC identifier, and the publisher page and supplement PDF did not retrieve. The bioRxiv preprint (PPR1213133, CC-BY) full text and JATS XML returned HTTP 429 twice and was not retrieved, so I could not read a data availability statement or a supplementary table list.

a1_downloadable.note: Open and free: I downloaded two mmCIF coordinate files from files.rcsb.org with no login. Maps are in EMDB.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL. The deposition is atomic coordinates only. There is no outcome column anywhere: any label (binding strength, silencing efficiency, mismatch tolerance) would have to be built from scratch, and this paper measured none at scale.

a3_inputs_present.note: Sequences are literally in the files: Vipr protein, the guide RNA (vrRNA), and both DNA strands appear as one-letter sequences in the entity_poly block.

a4_units_stated.note: Coordinates in Angstroms, resolution in Angstroms, both standard in mmCIF. Moot, since there is no measured label to carry units.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL. 18 deposited structures (21 maps claimed in the abstract), all of the same complex in different states and subunit counts. The checklist needs about 1,500 labelled rows, or 400 for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.note: Two files totalled 3 MB; all 18 would be roughly 15 MB. Trivially fits 16 GB RAM.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Abstract says 21 cryo-EM structures; the DOI-linked PDB search returns 18 atomic models. Explainable as a few map-only depositions, but I could not confirm without the paywalled methods.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL by construction. No physical measurement of any outcome is deposited, so the only available 'labels' (base pairs, contacts, triplex geometry) are computed from the same coordinates that would be the features: textbook leakage.

backbone.name: None applicable at this data size

integration.partner_dataset: None identified that would rescue it
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Could not be written: with 18 structures of one complex there is nothing to join on that creates examples.

honest_claim_h3: No honest model claim is possible from this paper's data: 18 cryo-electron microscopy structures of one protein-RNA-DNA complex support mechanistic description, not a trained predictor.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a guide RNA sequence and a candidate DNA sequence to predict whether this ancient CRISPR ancestor will bind and silence it.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would need many guide-RNA/DNA-target pairs with a measured binding or silencing readout. This paper supplies 18 atomic structures of a single complex, which is not a training set of any size.
plain_idea.predict: Whether a given double-stranded DNA site is recognised, given a VIPR guide RNA whose code skips every third base. The true answer would have to come from a binding or transcription-silencing assay, which this paper does not report in high throughput.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups building new programmable DNA-binding tools would want a targeting-rule predictor for a non-CRISPR recognition code; even a failed model would show whether the skip-every-third-base rule is the whole story. None of that is reachable from structures alone.

ml_idea: None viable from this paper. The structures are a beautiful mechanistic result (a gapped RNA-DNA hybrid that wraps the non-target strand into a triplex) but they are 18 snapshots of one complex, with no measured outcome variable. The nearest real ML project lives in the companion discovery paper (Science 10.1126/science.aei0498, in PubMed Central), which reports a genome-wide survey of natural VIPR guide RNAs and their targets plus phage-defence and silencing assays; evaluate that paper instead if a VIPR targeting-code predictor is wanted.

effort.compute_note: Measured, not estimated: two downloaded mmCIF files are 0.96 MB and 2.08 MB, and all 18 entries hold 282,173 atoms in total, so the whole dataset is about 15 MB. Compute was never the constraint; the number of examples is.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the labelled examples. One RCSB query on the paper's DOI returns 18 entries and no outcome column - that took two minutes and killed it.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A on three counts, all verified in the deposited files rather than read off the abstract. A5: 18 cryo-electron microscopy structures (21 maps claimed) of one Vipr-RNA-DNA complex, versus the ~1,500 rows the checklist requires. A2: there is no prediction target anywhere in the deposition, only atomic coordinates, so any label would have to be constructed from scratch. A8: the only labels derivable here (base pairs, contacts, triplex geometry) are computed from the same coordinates that would serve as features, which is leakage by construction. The data is genuinely open and tiny (about 15 MB, two files downloaded and parsed cleanly), so the rejection is about there being nothing to learn from, not about access or size. The companion paper 10.1126/science.aei0498 holds the functional and bioinformatic data and is the one worth evaluating.
